'''Hongkun Park''' (born 1967; {{Korean|hangul=박홍근}}) is a South Korean-born American chemist and physicist. He was appointed Corporate President of [[Samsung Electronics]] in January 2026 and serves as Head of the [[Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology]] (SAIT).<ref>{{cite web |title=Samsung Electronics Announces New Leadership |url=https://news.samsungsemiconductor.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-2/ }}</ref>

He is also the Mark Hyman Jr. Professor of Chemistry and a Professor of Physics at [[Harvard University]] (on leave).<ref name=HP1>{{cite web |title=Hongkun Park |url=https://www.chemistry.harvard.edu/people/hongkun-park |website=Harvard Department of Chemistry & Chemical Biology |access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref> Park is renowned for his contributions to nanoscience, [[quantum information science]], quantum materials, and bio–nano interfaces.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hongkun Park |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/hongkun-park |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |date=2025 |access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Park received a B.S. in chemistry from [[Seoul National University]] in 1990, graduating ''summa cum laude'' and as valedictorian. After completing his mandatory military service in the South Korean Army, he earned a Ph.D. in chemistry at [[Stanford University]] in 1996 under Richard N. Zare, then conducted postdoctoral research at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] and [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] with A. Paul Alivisatos and Paul L. McEuen.<ref name=HP1 />

== Career ==
Park joined the Harvard faculty in 1999 as an assistant professor. He became John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Natural Sciences in 2003 and was promoted to Full Professor in 2004. He holds joint appointments in Chemistry and Physics and is affiliated with the Harvard Quantum Science and Engineering Program, the Center for Brain Science,<ref name=HP1 /><ref>{{cite web|title=Hongkun Park – Center for Brain Science|url=https://cbs.fas.harvard.edu/directory/hongkun-park/|website=Harvard University|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref> and the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hongkun Park|url=https://www.broadinstitute.org/bios/hongkun-park|website=Broad Institute|date=3 April 2013 |access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>

== Research ==
Park’s early work pioneered single-molecule transistors and electron transport phenomena in nanoscale systems. In 2000, his team reported nanomechanical oscillations in a C<sub>60</sub> single-molecule transistor,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Park|first1=H.|last2=Park|first2=J.|last3=Lim|first3=A. K. L.|last4=Anderson|first4=E. H.|last5=Alivisatos|first5=A. P.|last6=McEuen|first6=P. L.|title=Nanomechanical oscillations in a single-C60 transistor|journal=Nature|year=2000|volume=407|issue=6800 |pages=57–60|doi=10.1038/35024031 |pmid=10993069 }}</ref> and in 2002, they observed a gate-tunable Kondo resonance in a single-molecule transistor.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Liang|first1=W.|last2=Shores|first2=M. P.|last3=Bockrath|first3=M.|last4=Long|first4=J. R.|last5=Park|first5=H.|title=Kondo resonance in a single-molecule transistor|journal=Nature|year=2002|volume=417|issue=6890 |pages=725–729|doi=10.1038/nature00790 |pmid=12066180 |bibcode=2002Natur.417..725L }}</ref>

He has also contributed to quantum sensing and nanoscale NMR. A 2016 ''Science'' paper co-authored by Park demonstrated room-temperature nuclear magnetic resonance detection and spectroscopy of single proteins using a diamond-based quantum sensor.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lovchinsky|first1=I.|last2=Sushkov|first2=A. O.|last3=Urbach|first3=E.|last4=de Leon|first4=N. P.|last5=Choi|first5=S.|last6=de Greve|first6=K.|last7=Evans|first7=R.|last8=Gertner|first8=R.|last9=Bersin|first9=E.|last10=Müller|first10=C.|last11=McGuinness|first11=L.|last12=Jelezko|first12=F.|last13=Walsworth|first13=R. L.|last14=Park|first14=H.|last15=Lukin|first15=M. D.|title=Nuclear magnetic resonance detection and spectroscopy of single proteins using quantum logic|journal=Science|year=2016|volume=351|issue=6275|pages=836–841|doi=10.1126/science.aad8022 |pmid=26847544 |bibcode=2016Sci...351..836L |url=http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:34744143 }}</ref>

In two-dimensional semiconductor heterostructures, Park’s group has studied correlated electron phases, including the formation of bilayer Wigner crystals in transition-metal dichalcogenide heterostructures.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Zhou|first1=Y.|last2=Sung|first2=J.|last3=Brutschea|first3=E.|last4=Esterlis|first4=I.|last5=Wang|first5=Y.|last6=Scuri|first6=G.|last7=Gelly|first7=R. J.|last8=Heo|first8=H.|last9=Taniguchi|first9=T.|last10=Watanabe|first10=K.|last11=Zaránd|first11=G.|last12=Lukin|first12=M. D.|last13=Kim|first13=P.|last14=Demler|first14=E.|last15=Park|first15=H.|title=Bilayer Wigner crystals in a transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructure|journal=Nature|year=2021|volume=595|issue=7865 |pages=48–52|doi=10.1038/s41586-021-03560-w |pmid=34194017 |arxiv=2010.03037 |bibcode=2021Natur.595...48Z }}</ref>

Park has also developed novel nano–bio interfaces. His laboratory demonstrated vertical silicon nanoneedles capable of delivering biomolecules into living cells,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Shalek|first1=A. K.|last2=Robinson|first2=J. T.|last3=Karp|first3=E. S.|last4=Lee|first4=J. S.|last5=Ahn|first5=D.-R.|last6=Yoon|first6=M.-H.|last7=Sutton|first7=A.|last8=Jorgolli|first8=M.|last9=Gertner|first9=R. S.|last10=Gujral|first10=T. S.|last11=MacBeath|first11=G.|last12=Yang|first12=E. G.|last13=Park|first13=H.|title=Vertical silicon nanowires as a universal platform for delivering biomolecules into living cells|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=107|issue=5|pages=1870–1875|year=2010|doi=10.1073/pnas.0909350107 |pmc=2836617}}</ref> and later developed CMOS nanoelectrode arrays that enable molecular delivery and intracellular recording of neurons and cardiomyocytes.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Abbott|first1=J.|last2=Ye|first2=T.|last3=Qin|first3=L.|last4=Jorgolli|first4=M.|last5=Gertner|first5=R. S.|last6=Ham|first6=D.|last7=Park|first7=H.|title=CMOS nanoelectrode array for all-electrical intracellular electrophysiological imaging|journal=Nature Nanotechnology|volume=12|pages=460–466|year=2017|issue=5 |doi=10.1038/nnano.2017.15 |pmid=28288116 |pmc=5420310 }}</ref> He also contributed to the development of early pipelines for single-cell RNA sequencing.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Shalek|first1=A. K.|last2=Satija|first2=R.|last3=Adiconis|first3=X.|last4=Gertner|first4=R. S.|last5=Gaublomme|first5=J. T.|last6=Raychowdhury|first6=R.|last7=Schwartz|first7=S.|last8=Yosef|first8=N.|last9=Malboeuf|first9=C.|last10=Gnirke|first10=A.|last11=Goren|first11=A.|last12=Hacohen|first12=N.|last13=Levin|first13=J. Z.|last14=Park|first14=H.|last15=Regev|first15=A.|title=Single-cell transcriptomics reveals bimodality in expression and splicing in immune cells|journal=Nature|volume=498|pages=236–240|year=2013|issue=7453 |doi=10.1038/nature12172 |pmid=23685454 |bibcode=2013Natur.498..236S |url=http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:11879192 |pmc=3683364}}</ref>

He is also known for his invention of novel scanned-probe techniques to help characterize his solution-based synthesis of transition-metal-oxide nanostructures.<ref name="Ho-Am_Foundation-1" />

== Honors and awards ==
Park’s recognitions include:
* [[Ho-Am Prize in Science]] (2003).<ref name="Ho-Am_Foundation-1">{{cite web|title=Previous Laureates – Science (2003)|url=https://www.hoamfoundation.org/eng/award/part_view.asp?idx=61|website=Ho-Am Foundation|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>
* [[Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering]] (2001).<ref>{{cite web|title=Park, Hongkun — Packard Fellows|url=https://www.packard.org/fellow/park-hongkun/|website=The David and Lucile Packard Foundation|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>
* [[NIH Director's Pioneer Award]] (2008).<ref>{{cite news|last=Powell|first=Alvin|title=NIH selects nine Pioneers, Innovators from Harvard|url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2008/09/nih-selects-nine-pioneers-innovators-from-harvard/|work=Harvard Gazette|date=25 September 2008|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>
* [[Vannevar Bush]] Faculty Fellowship (2016).<ref>{{cite web|title=2016 Vannevar Bush Faculty Fellows|url=https://basicresearch.defense.gov/Programs/Vannevar-Bush-Faculty-Fellowship/2016-Vannevar-Bush-Fellows/|website=U.S. Department of Defense – Basic Research|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>
* Elected Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (2011).<ref>{{cite news|title=2011 AAAS Fellows announced|url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-names-2011-fellows|website=AAAS|date=2011|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>
* Member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2025).<ref>{{cite web|title=Hongkun Park|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/hongkun-park|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|date=2025|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>

== Editorial and professional service ==
Park has served as an associate editor of ''[[Nano Letters]]'' and on advisory boards for journals such as ''Chemical Society Reviews,'' ''Chemical Science,'' and ''Physical Review Applied.''<ref>{{cite web|title=Hongkun Park|url=https://www.broadinstitute.org/bios/hongkun-park|website=Broad Institute|date=3 April 2013 |access-date=2025-09-06}}{{cite web|title=Editors of Physical Review Applied|url=https://journals.aps.org/prapplied/staff#edboard}}</ref> He has been a member of the jury for the [[BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Awards]] in Basic Sciences.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hongkun Park — Jury Member|url=https://www.frontiersofknowledgeawards-fbbva.es/jurado/hongkun-park-2/|website=BBVA Foundation — Frontiers of Knowledge Awards|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref>

== Entrepreneurship ==
Park is a scientific co-founder of Quantum Diamond Technologies, Inc. (QDTI), which develops diamond-based quantum sensors,<ref>{{cite web|title=Hongkun Park — QDTI|url=https://qdti.com/team/hongkun-park|website=Quantum Diamond Technologies|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref> and of CytoTronics, a Harvard spin-out developing semiconductor platforms for cell-based assays.<ref>{{cite press release|title=CytoTronics Launches with $9.25 Million in Seed Funding to Revolutionize Drug Discovery and Phenotypic Screening|url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220428005157/en/CytoTronics-Launches-with-%249.25-Million-in-Seed-Funding-to-Revolutionize-Drug-Discovery-and-Phenotypic-Screening|work=Business Wire|date=28 April 2022|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=CytoTronics launches to tackle drug discovery and phenotypic screening|url=https://otd.harvard.edu/news/cytotronics-launches-to-tackle-drug-discovery-and-phenotypic-screening/|website=Harvard Office of Technology Development|date=2022|access-date=2025-09-06}}</ref> Since 2021, he has served as a senior advisor for [[Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology]].
